judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's values and classifications are all correct. I re-derived them: problem 1's parallelogram gives 5x = 75 and x = 15 (the TikZ places (5x) at A and 75 at C, which are opposite vertices, so the opposite-angle property is the right one); problem 2's 8x+40 = 360 gives x = 40 with angles 60, 80, 110, 110; problem 3's square gives 3x-5 = x+7 and x = 6; problem 4's congruent bisecting diagonals give a rectangle with 4x-6 = x+9, x = 5 and JL = 14; problem 5's rhombus puts 90 + (4x-6) + 2x in one triangle, so x = 16 with 32 + 58 + 90 = 180; and problem 6's A(-2,1), B(2,3), C(4,-1) give slopes 1/2 and -2 with both lengths sqrt(20) = 4.47, so square. Two things the judge's clean sweep missed. (1) The focus skill is unverified. The task focus is 'classifying quadrilaterals from defining properties' and every one of problems 1-6 opens by asking for the most specific NAME, but verify.json records only the algebra for those ids and declares manual entries solely for problems 7 and 8; the names (parallelogram, quadrilateral, square, rectangle, rhombus, square) appear only in the key's prose and never in the Quick Answers bank, which prints '1. 15', '3. 6', '4. 5, 14'. (2) A visual defect in the study guide: in Skill 1's example figure the two angle labels collide in the middle of the parallelogram and print as the run '(3x + 8)deg 62deg', neither one adjacent to its own vertex. I rendered it at 400 dpi to confirm. The worksheet's problem 1 uses the same figure at scale 0.85 and renders cleanly, so the fault is the study guide's scale=0.5 copy keeping absolute label offsets (angle radius=6mm, angle eccentricity=1.9 and 1.7) on a figure only about 1.2 cm tall. The overprint gate passed because the boxes sit side by side rather than overlapping.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 2 is the item most quadrilateral sets get wrong: a figure with NO marks, where the correct classification is 'quadrilateral' and the key defends it -- 'it may happen to be a trapezoid, but the figure does not say so, and a name has to be forced by the given properties, not guessed from the drawing' -- with a teaching note that no pair of the computed angles sums to 180, confirming no parallel sides.

The three classification routes are genuinely different evidence types rather than restatements: marks on a figure (1, 3), diagonal behaviour (4, 5), and vertex coordinates (6), which is what makes the 'most specific name' instruction bite differently each time.

Problem 4's figure is deliberately drawn misleading and labelled 'Not to scale', and the key names the trap it sets: 'Listen for: "the picture looks like a rectangle, so I did not need the diagonals."'

Problem 7 asks for an always/sometimes/never judgement AND a mark to add to the figure, and its manual desc captures both halves, including the drawn part -- 'the student must name the defining property that separates the two families and mark on the given rhombus what would have to be added' -- with the key noting that answering 'never' forgets the square.

Problem 8's model argument is a complete proof rather than a name-drop: diagonal QS, alternate interior angles, reflexive QS, SAS, then CPCTC to reach both pairs of opposite sides congruent, and it closes by refusing the rectangle upgrade for want of any angle constraint.

root_causes.description: The classification answer -- the skill this worksheet exists to teach -- is not machine-checkable by any type verify.py supports (there is no name/choice type), and it was not declared manual either, so on six of eight problems only the incidental algebra is covered. Per-id coverage is satisfied by the solve/eval entries, so nothing in the chain notices.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 1: 'Name the most specific quadrilateral these marks force, then use that family's angle property to find x'; problems 3, 4 and 5 open with the same 'Name the most specific quadrilateral' request; problem 2 asks 'Say what that means about naming it'; problem 6 ends 'give the most specific name for ABCD, saying which computed fact forces each part of that name'.
verify.json ids 1-6 contain only solve, eval, slope and distance entries; the only 'manual' entries in the file are ids 7 and 8.

scripts/verify.py check_problem dispatches manual, distance, midpoint, slope, polygon_area, compare, solve, eval, approx and triangle -- there is no type that can check the string 'rectangle', so manual is the only honest declaration for these answers.

answer_key.pdf carries the classifications only in prose ('Step 1. Classify.'), and the Quick Answers bank prints '1. 15', '2. 40', '3. 6', '4. 5, 14', '5. 16', '6. 1/2, -2, 4.47, 4.47' -- not one shape name, although the name is the first thing each problem asks for.

root_causes.description: TikZ angle-label placement uses absolute lengths (angle radius in mm, multiplied by angle eccentricity) that do not scale with the picture's scale factor, so re-using a worksheet figure at a smaller scale in the study guide drives both labels toward the centre until they collide. The overprint gate cannot catch it because the word boxes abut rather than overlap.
evidence: study_guide.tex Skill 1 example: tikzpicture[scale=0.5] with '\pic [draw, angle radius=6mm, angle eccentricity=1.9 ... "$(3x + 8)^\circ$"] {angle = B--A--D}' and '\pic [draw, angle radius=6mm, angle eccentricity=1.7 ... "$62^\circ$"] {angle = D--C--B}'. The parallelogram is 2.415 units tall, i.e. about 1.2 cm at scale 0.5, while each label is pushed 10-11 mm from its vertex.

study_guide.pdf page 1 rendered at 400 dpi: '(3x + 8)deg' and '62deg' print immediately adjacent at mid-height, with the A arc at the lower left and the C arc at the upper right, so neither label sits by its own arc; pdftotext returns them as the single run '(3x + 8)circ62circ'.

worksheet.tex problem 1 draws the same parallelogram at scale=0.85 with angle radius=7mm and renders cleanly -- (5x) beside A's arc, 75 beside C's arc -- confirming the difference is the scale factor, not the geometry.
gate_log.txt reports 'overprint PASS'; tests/check_overprint.py measures overlap area as a fraction of the smaller word box, so adjacent-but-not-overlapping labels are invisible to it.

improvements.title: Cover the 'most specific name' answer in problems 1-6 with manual entries so the focus skill is graded
improvements.proposed_change: Require a check per requested response rather than per problem id, and enforce it in the gate chain: count the requests inside each \problem body ('Name the', 'Say what', 'give the most specific name', lettered parts) and fail when an id's request count exceeds its verify-entry count. For this sheet that adds six manual entries whose desc states the expected classification and the property that forces it (parallelogram from two pairs of parallel sides; quadrilateral because no marks force more; square from four congruent sides plus a right angle; rectangle from congruent bisecting diagonals; rhombus from congruent sides with perpendicular bisecting diagonals; square from perpendicular AND congruent adjacent sides). Separately, have render_quick_answers include a manual entry's short expected name in the bank, so the grader sees 'rectangle' beside '5, 14' instead of the algebra alone.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: a problem body reading 'Name the most specific quadrilateral these marks force, then use that family's angle property to find x' with a verify id holding only a solve entry -- the checker must exit non-zero naming the uncovered request, and pass once a manual entry is added. curr-331 builds green today (layout-ws PASS, verify-ws MANUAL from ids 7 and 8 only), so the assertion fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: The answer the worksheet asks for FIRST in six of eight problems stops being the one thing nobody checks, the reported manual count rises from 2 to 8, and the answer key gains an explicit grading standard for each classification instead of leaving it implicit in the solution prose.
improvements.risk: Request counting over-fires on narrative prose and must be scoped to \problem bodies with an author override; back-filling the corpus will surface many similar ids at once, and adding names to the Quick Answers bank widens rows, which feeds column_count and the answer-key page budget.

improvements.title: Scale TikZ angle-label offsets with the picture scale so the study-guide figure's two labels stop colliding
improvements.proposed_change: Stop hard-coding absolute label offsets in scaled pictures. Provide a macro in templates/figure-macros.tex that takes the picture's scale factor and sets angle radius and angle eccentricity proportionally (or uses 'transform shape' plus scale-relative units), and document in references/latex-templates.md that a figure re-used at a smaller scale must have its angle radius reduced by the same factor -- here the study guide's scale=0.5 copy should use roughly a 3.5 mm radius, or place the two labels outside the quadrilateral. Add near-collision detection to tests/check_overprint.py: flag two word boxes whose vertical spans overlap and whose horizontal gap is under about one space width, which is the shape this defect takes.
improvements.regression_test: In tests/test_overprint.py add a fixture reproducing the curr-331 study-guide figure (scale=0.5 parallelogram, angle radius=6mm, eccentricity 1.9 and 1.7, labels '(3x + 8)^\circ' and '62^\circ'): compile it and assert check_overprint.py exits non-zero on the near-collision, and that the scale-corrected variant exits 0. The current checker passes both, so the assertion fails before the change and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: The first worked example a student reads in this study guide stops being ambiguous about which angle is 62 degrees, and every future scaled-down re-use of a worksheet figure keeps its labels attached to their vertices; the overprint gate gains coverage of a collision class it currently cannot see.
improvements.risk: A near-collision threshold risks false positives on legitimately tight math typesetting (subscripts, adjacent inline symbols), so it needs calibration against the existing corpus in the same way the current overlap threshold was, and should start as a warning before it becomes a failure.

case_summary: Mathematically correct and pedagogically well-aimed: all twelve tagged checks re-derive (x = 15, 40, 6, 5 with JL = 14, 16, and the coordinate square with slopes 1/2 and -2 and both sides sqrt(20) = 4.47), the classifications the key gives are the most specific ones the evidence forces in every case, and problems 2 and 4 are unusually good because one has no marks at all and the other draws a deliberately misleading figure. Two defects the judge did not reach. First, the focus skill is unverified: problems 1-6 all ask for the most specific NAME, and only the algebra is recorded, with the names appearing solely in the key's prose and never in the Quick Answers bank -- and since verify.py has no type that can check a name, the honest declaration is manual, as problems 7 and 8 correctly use. Second, the study guide's Skill 1 example figure prints its two angle labels on top of one another in the middle of the parallelogram because the scale=0.5 picture keeps absolute 6 mm/1.9 label offsets; the same figure at scale 0.85 on the worksheet is clean, and the overprint gate misses it because the labels abut rather than overlap.
